title: Fix two typo'd words.
description:
Somehow "accomodate" and "assymetric" snuck into our wireshark_words.txt list.
They should be "accommodate" and "asymmetric".

Remove them and fix the corresponding typos in the codebase -- two in field
names, one in a user-visible string in an NCSI field value enumeration, one in
a preprocessor macro, one in a variable name, and the rest in comments.

The field "smb2.share_caps.assymetric" is now "smb2.share_caps.asymmetric" and
"sprt.payload.msg_init.assym_data_types" is now
"sprt.payload.msg_init.asymm_data_types".

notes.body: Are any of those ASN.1 files just copies of the official ASN.1 specification for that protocol?  If so, we might not want to fix them.

Thanks for the question!

The non-whitespace modifications to those files are all in a header which appears to be Wireshark-specific, which it seems safe to assume is not part of the source material.

The trailing whitespace is (I guess) being cleaned up by our EditorConfig settings (`trim_trailing_whitespace = true`).  Should we consider tweaking that config so that trailing whitespace is preserved for these paths?  Or do you prefer that we allow the whitespace to be zapped?
assigned to @martin.r.mathieson
resolved all threads

I think this change is fine - the .asn file diffs are in the hand-written preamble rather than copied from the specs.  And it's preferable to strip out trailing whitespace (where you were there anyway).

Thanks for picking up those errors in wireshark_words.txt.  I resisted checking comments in dissector code until it became difficult to find any errors in literal strings in the code. I am tempted now to add 'check_spelling.py --commits 1 --comments' to the pipeline, and hopefully avoid doing many more tedious scans of the entire dissectors folder.  Does this seem reasonable?

Thanks Martin!

> I am tempted now to add 'check_spelling.py --commits 1 --comments' to the pipeline, and hopefully avoid doing many more tedious scans of the entire dissectors folder. Does this seem reasonable?

I'm not sufficiently familiar with the overall workflow (and its potential impacts) to form any strong opinion on that.

In general I'm in favor of pre-commit checks but mindful of not wanting to put more hurdles in front of potential contributors.  Perhaps having maintainers/volunteers do occasional tedious spell-check scans is the price we pay for being as welcoming as possible towards contributors who might have highly specialized protocol knowledge and be great at coding but less great at English spelling.

I'm also mindful of avoiding a situation where contributors have to "satisfy the spell checker" before their potentially correct code can be accepted.  Can the pipeline be made to raise a warning instead of causing a failure -- and have that warning somehow visible in the pipeline's status -- or is that not a capability we have?  I'm not even sure if that would be truly helpful.  Just thinking out loud, really. :smile:

BTW, I discovered these two typos in `wireshark_words.txt` by running the [Wikipedia list of common misspellings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Lists_of_common_misspellings/For_machines) across our codebase.  Happy to share my python script if you are interested.  The [other list on Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:AWB/Typos) might be a step too far...

The pipeline only fails if a called script returns a non-zero code (some of the other checking scripts have warnings that can be made, but only what are judged to be errors will cause a non-zero exit code).  My thought was that reviewers (and contributors who look at the pipeline output) can quickly see these.  Sometimes pointing out something trivial from the pipeline is a convenient way to tell someone that their change will be reviewed.

Dissectors use lots of abbreviations and acronyms in item labels and display filters. There are also lots of company names and foreign spellings of words that should not be "corrected".  One thing I considered was to use SpellChecker.correction() or SpellChecker.candidates(), then only report words that are (by some measure) really quite close to proper words.  I made a comment that these functions are slow, but if they can cut down on the time taken to trawl through output, maybe worth it?

Those Wikipedia pages are interesting.. I suspect I won't add spelling to the pipeline at the moment though - I don't have much available time right now.
Please do share your script.

Attached [check-for-wikipedia-typos.py](/uploads/48df86047ffe3534d85fb885a62774ef/check-for-wikipedia-typos.py).  It still needs some polish -- some command-line parsing, and perhaps some more meaningful structure -- but it is quite effective.  Still throws out a few false positives and finds some things we can't/shouldn't change, but it does find a good number of real typos, including some which will be user-visible.  Run it and look for `../output.patch` with the suggested fixes.

I did this:
![image](/uploads/007075e216ca69065462ef991a858a21/image.png)
to make sure there were no other bad words in wireshark_words.txt

Ha, I didn't even need to create bad_words - could have used db directly.  I am usually quite careful when adding dictionary words.

Am running your full script now.  Might as well fix these up.  It might be that we'd want to (optionally?) fetch the wrongly-spelt words from the page then check for them being used in check_spelling.py

It turns out that what I probably want to do is to get the first words into a list, then add to check_spelling.py:

spell.word_frequency.remove_words(bad_words)

Will try 'patch -s -p0 < output.patch' and will create an MR out of what is valid first.  Cool script!

Fix two typo'd words.

Somehow "accomodate" and "assymetric" snuck into our wireshark_words.txt list.
They should be "accommodate" and "asymmetric".

Remove them and fix the corresponding typos in the codebase -- two in field
names, one in a user-visible string in an NCSI field value enumeration, one in
a preprocessor macro, one in a variable name, and the rest in comments.

The field "smb2.share_caps.assymetric" is now "smb2.share_caps.asymmetric" and
"sprt.payload.msg_init.assym_data_types" is now
"sprt.payload.msg_init.asymm_data_types".
